why: BAs map processes to find waste and design the target. BPMN is the standard notation recruiters mention, and a clear diagram in your portfolio stands out.
outcome: read and draw BPMN diagrams with events, tasks, gateways and swimlanes, and use them to improve a process.

lessons.title: The core symbols
text: BPMN has many symbols, but about ten cover most diagrams. Events (circles) start and end things, activities (rounded rectangles) are work, gateways (diamonds) split or join paths, arrows show the order.
A diagram reads left to right, from one start event to one or more end events.
points: Start event: thin circle. End event: thick circle. Intermediate events: double circle (e.g. a timer).
Task: one unit of work done by a person or system, named verb + object ('Check application').
Exclusive gateway (X): exactly one path, based on a condition.
Parallel gateway (+): all paths happen; a second + waits for all of them.
Sequence flow (solid arrow) inside a pool; message flow (dashed) between pools.

lessons.title: Pools, lanes and a full example
text: A pool is a participant (your company, a client). Lanes split a pool by role or department, so you see who does what and where handoffs happen.
Handoffs between lanes are where delays and errors usually hide.
points: One lane per role: Candidate, Recruiter, Hiring manager.
Label gateway paths with the condition ('Profile fits?' → Yes / No).
Keep one level of detail per diagram; use sub-processes for details.
Tools: draw.io (free), Bizagi Modeler, Camunda Modeler, Visio, Miro.

example.code:
Pool: Recruitment
 Lane Candidate : (Start: applies online) -> [Submit CV]
 Lane Recruiter : [Screen CV] -> <X Profile fits?>
                     No  -> [Send rejection] -> (End: rejected)
                     Yes -> [Schedule interview]
 Lane Manager   : [Interview] -> <X Hire?>
                     Yes -> [Send offer] -> (End: hired)
                     No  -> [Send rejection] -> (End: rejected)

lessons.title: From as-is to to-be
text: Map the as-is process with the people who do it, not from the procedure manual. Then measure: volumes, time per step, waiting time, error rate.
Design the to-be by removing waste: unnecessary approvals, duplicate data entry, waiting between lanes, rework loops.
points: Mark pain points directly on the diagram.
Look for loops back (rework) and long waits at handoffs.
Automate repetitive, rule-based tasks; keep judgement with people.
Validate the to-be with the same people before writing stories.

lessons.title: Events, timers and a model people can read
text: Beyond tasks and gateways, events show what happens to a process: a message arrives, a deadline passes, an error occurs. A timer attached to the edge of a task (a boundary event) handles 'if this takes more than 5 days, then...' without cluttering the diagram.

A model is a communication tool. Name tasks verb + object ('Check stock'), name end events with the result ('Order shipped'), keep one level of detail per diagram, and use sub-processes to hide the details of a complex step. Validate the model by walking through real cases with the people who do the work.
points: Message events: something comes from or goes to another participant (pool).
Error and escalation events show what happens when a step fails.
Every path must reach an end event; label the gateway outflows.
About 15 to 20 elements per diagram; more means a sub-process is needed.

example.code:
(Start: order received)
  → [Check stock]
  → <X> in stock?
       yes → [Ship order] → (End: order shipped)
       no  → [Order from supplier]
               ⏱ boundary timer 5 days on the task → [Notify customer of delay]
               → [Ship order] → (End: order shipped)
Message flow: [Order from supplier] ⇢ Supplier pool
example.note: The timer handles the delay case without a second copy of the process.

items: Single unit of work, verb + object
Done by a person / by a system
One path based on a condition
All paths, then wait for all
A role or department in a pool
Order of steps in a pool

pitfalls: Too much detail in one diagram: nobody reads it.
Mapping the official procedure instead of what people really do.
Mixing systems and roles in the same lanes without clear names.

exercises.q: Which gateway do you use when both 'Check references' and 'Prepare contract' happen at the same time after the offer is accepted?
exercises.answer: A parallel gateway (+) to split, and another parallel gateway to join before the next step, which waits until both are done.

exercises.q: Name three signs of waste on an as-is diagram.
exercises.answer: Rework loops going back to earlier steps, long waiting times at handoffs between lanes, and the same data being entered in several systems. Also: approvals that never reject anything.
Use verb + object: 'Screen CV', 'Conduct interview', 'Approve hiring'. Roles belong to lanes, not task names.

exercises.q: Review this model and list what you would fix: tasks named 'Stock', 'Supplier' and 'Mail', an exclusive gateway with unlabelled outflows, and one path that stops at a task with no end event.
exercises.answer: Rename tasks as verb + object: 'Check stock', 'Order from supplier', 'Email the customer'. Label each gateway outflow with its condition (in stock: yes / no) and phrase the gateway as a question. Add an end event named with the result on the path that stops, so every path ends. Also check that the gateway that splits the flow is matched where the paths join again if needed.

interview.q: Why use BPMN rather than a simple flowchart?
interview.a: It is a standard understood by business and IT, it shows who does what with pools and lanes, distinguishes kinds of events and gateways precisely, and can even be executed by workflow engines.

interview.q: How do you map an as-is process?
interview.a: Interview and observe the people who do the work, map step by step with them, capture volumes, timings and pain points, then validate the diagram with them before analysing it.
An exclusive gateway sends the flow down exactly one path based on a condition. A parallel gateway activates all outgoing paths at once and, when joining, waits for all of them.

interview.q: How do you make sure a process model is correct?
interview.a: I walk through it with the people who do the work, using real recent cases, including exceptions: what happens if a document is missing, a deadline passes or a system is down. I check that every path ends, gateways are labelled, names are clear verb plus object, and the level of detail suits the audience. I update the model until the people doing the job recognise their process.
